verdict: The best photograph in the set and the worst piece of data in it. It's the only frame where the camera picked one human being and committed — full-frame, red tank, arms open, drum line thrown out of focus behind him. Every wide shot in this corpus tells you about the drill; this one tells you about a body. If I could keep one frame, it's this. If I had to build from one frame, it's absolutely not this.

The teal wedge driving through white ranks beats the Cavaliers' letterform every time. One is a shape you read instantly and can hold in your head; the other is a word you have to spell out. Field writing is a magic trick that stops being magic the instant the audience finishes reading it. A wedge stays a wedge for the whole phrase.

Same corps, same show, two overhead wides — one with the guard smeared into gold streaks, one pin sharp. The blurred one is the better picture and the worse chart, and I'd keep the blur without hesitating. A perfectly sharp overhead of a drill set is a spreadsheet with grass on it. The smear is the only evidence in the frame that anything is actually happening.

The wide of crouched brown figures scattered on green — the one where you genuinely can't tell what you're looking at for a beat — is worth more than the polished close-up of the same show's guard smiling behind a flag. Uncertainty is the scarcest resource in this whole corpus. Everything else here is competent and fully legible on contact, and legible-on-contact is exactly the thing I don't need more of.

A member flat on the ground beside a rack of drums, another standing over them, empty night stadium, three-quarters of the corps still upright in the background. I cannot tell whether that's choreography or a collapse, and that is precisely why it's the strongest frame in the set. If someone tells me which it is, the frame gets worse. Do not resolve it.

This beats the wide of the same show without argument. Bodies planted on orange ramps at three heights, horns up, one guard member sprinting through frame in the opposite direction — it's the only frame in the corpus where the props are structural rather than scenic. A ramp is a coordinate system with a z-axis. Everything else here is people on a plane. If I'm building from one frame, it's this one.

Sabotaged by its own equipment. The most interesting objects in the picture are four sousaphone bells parked in the near foreground, and they're interesting by accident — they eat the bottom third and turn the actual performance into a distant smear under a sponsor banner. A frame where the gear outranks the drill is a frame about logistics.

Three separated blocks with the fifty yard line left completely empty between them, and the empty middle is the subject. A drill that vacates the most valuable real estate on the field is making a claim, and it's a claim you can read from the press box in one second. Better than a full field of even distribution — unevenness is the information.

One dense knot of bodies collapsed at the fifty while eighty people lie flat and scattered across the rest of the turf like debris. Reads as aftermath. It's the best of the high wides because the crowd in the near seats gives the emptiness a scale — you can see how much field is being deliberately wasted. Crown's version has the same altitude and none of the risk.

Yesterday I claimed the illegible wide from this show was worth more than the legible frames, and here's the test: same corps, mid-field, everything resolved — you can count the horn line, identify the flags, read the drill. It's fine and it's inert. The other frame made me work for a beat and I still don't fully know what I saw. This one I finished in half a second. Confirms the call.

A raised fist in the bottom-right corner, in silhouette, out of focus, belonging to nobody identifiable — and the corps a hundred yards off in a tight symmetric block. Better than any frame that records the field alone, because it's the only one that records reception. Star's scoreboard spelling SUMMER MUSIC GAMES in bulb matrix is the only frame where the stadium itself is typography, and I'd still trade it for the fist.

Forty guard members inverted mid-air simultaneously, red and orange, while the horn line stands planted in cream around them. This is the strongest frame I've been shown, and it settles something: on Monday I argued the Bluecoats ramp frame was the one to build from because a ramp is a coordinate system with a z-axis. This is the same axis with no hardware purchased. Bodies leaving the plane on their own beats bodies standing on a plane someone welded.

Same corps, one year apart, same altitude, and 2014 wins because it wastes the field on purpose — one dense knot at the fifty, guard scattered to the edges like debris — while 2013 distributes evenly across the whole hundred yards. Unevenness is the information. Third day running I've made this exact call, which means it's either a taste or a tic, and I'm now watching for the frame that makes me pick the even one.

The corps spells DCI on the field, which by my own rule is a magic trick that dies the second you finish reading it. But the near stands are a rainy scatter of open umbrellas, and that scatter is the better composition in the frame by a distance. Trade the letters, keep the crowd. The audience is the only thing in this picture that isn't following a chart.

A broadcast lower-third burned permanently into the bottom third, telling you which four bodies to look at out of two hundred. Worthless as drill data and the most honest frame in the set about how anyone actually experienced these shows — through a producer deciding where your attention goes. Keep it as evidence, never build from it.

Pastel rings on wheeled frames, everything close and fully legible. The rings are scenery: you look through them and the drill behind them is unaffected. The ramps in bloo-2014-t132 are structure: you stand on them and the whole coordinate system gains a dimension. Props that change where a body can be beat props that change what's behind it, every time.

One figure in a blue costume alone in a lot of grass, one shako in the corner. Isolated by emptiness, which is the weaker kind of isolation — the 1992 close-up commits to a single face while leaving an entire drum line blurred behind it, so you know precisely what's being ignored. This frame gives me no evidence anything else is happening at all.

This is the frame that makes me amend the rule instead of repeating it. Nine diagonal ranks spread evenly across the whole hundred yards — by my own standard three days running, even distribution should lose. It doesn't, because the unevenness isn't between the bodies, it's between the drill and the paint: the yard lines run one way and the ranks run another, and the friction between chart and stadium is the information. Unevenness survives. It just doesn't have to be unevenness among the dots.

Five men in white shirts carrying a sixth horizontally through the air over a wrought-iron prop. The only frame in this entire corpus where the members are handling each other rather than equipment — bodies as the apparatus. I called the 1992 solo close-up the best photograph in the set and I stand by it, but that one commits to a single face; this one commits to six people who physically cannot complete the picture alone. Hang the 1992. Build from this.

Same corps, same show, later in the run: the teal wedge has arrived and resolved into a symmetric block with a mascot flag planted at the center. It confirms the earlier call in the losing direction — the wedge was the whole show and this is merely what the wedge was for. General claim, and I'd like to be held to it: every frame in this corpus showing a form completed is worth less than the frame showing it forming. Arrival is a receipt. Approach is the event.

A dense diagonal mass of white uniforms, and the most interesting object in the picture is the Indiana University logo painted at midfield with the drill deliberately parting around it. This is field writing I finally like, because the corps didn't write it — the stadium did, and the drill has to negotiate with a mark it didn't make and can't move. Beats a corps spelling its own name every single time. A form that accommodates something is more interesting than a form that announces something.

Red scaffold cages with drummers threading between them and a rank of sousaphones jammed into the near edge. Third place in the props argument and I'll rank them: ramps you stand on (structural, adds an axis), cages you can be inside (containment, adds a boundary), rings you look through (scenery, adds nothing behind it). The cages beat the pastel rings. But nothing in this frame is wasted — it's crowded to all four edges, and a picture with no vacancy has nowhere to put emphasis.

Dice props scattered through the ranks with a broadcast chyron burned across the bottom naming the tune and the composer. Same class as the LHS lower-third — evidence of how these shows were watched, not of what they were. But here the caption is losing to its own content, because dice have faces and faces are readable from the press box, which is more than most props in this corpus can claim. Keep it for the dice. The chyron is just proof someone was directing your eye.

Maroon, gold and white bodies interpenetrating mid-transition, angles in every direction, nothing resolved. Set it against t760 — the same corps in an enormous symmetric flag array, finished and gorgeous — and t760 is the better photograph while t384 is the better second of the show. I've been claiming for two days that arrival is a receipt and approach is the event; this is the clean test and the messy one wins. Take the transition.

Twenty white sail-flags in a radial fan over ranks in maroon and gold, perfectly bilateral, the whole hundred yards accounted for. It is the most beautiful frame in today's set and I'd hang it without hesitating. But there is nothing in it left to happen — every question the drill asked has been answered in the same instant, and a picture with no unresolved force in it is a curtain call. Hang it. Don't build from it.

Four dispersed knots and a scatter of guard, with the Colts helmet painted at midfield left completely uncovered. The drill negotiated with a mark it didn't paint and can't move, which is the same reason I liked pr-2008-t168 — a form that accommodates something beats a form that announces something. Beats t184, where the same corps runs even ranks parallel to the yard lines: maximum agreement with the stadium is maximum silence.

Even ranks spread edge to edge, guard in orange along the front in a tidy row, the whole field used at uniform density. It loses twice by my own standards — no unevenness among the bodies, and no friction between the drill and the paint, because the ranks run exactly the way the yard lines do. This is the frame I'd have called competent in April and now can't find anything to want in.

Interlace tearing, comb artifacts, the entire image coming apart across a rank of sousaphones. The only frame in this corpus where the medium is visible, and that makes it more honest than any clean wide — a tape is how anybody actually got to see any of this in 1998. Better than lhs-1998-t438's illegible crouching figures, because that frame is uncertain about its subject while this one is certain about its subject and uncertain about its own survival. Keep permanently. Never build from it.

Three circles with a single figure planted at the center of the middle one, versus the same corps spelling a word in t296. The circles win the way shapes always beat words here — a circle stays a circle for the whole phrase and a word dies the instant you finish reading it. But I'll register the complaint: the circles are inert. Perfectly even, perfectly centered, negotiating with nothing on the field. Winning against field writing is a low bar and this frame clears it without doing anything else.

Two overheads, both from the top of the stadium, and this one wins because the guard is smeared into gold streaks. Set it against cadets-2021-t760 — the radial fan of white flags, bilaterally perfect, every yard accounted for — and t760 is unarguably the better photograph and the worse second. Blur is the only evidence in an overhead that time is passing. A pin-sharp aerial of a completed set is a spreadsheet with grass on it, and t760 is a very beautiful spreadsheet.

Interlace tearing across a rank of sousaphones, the whole image coming apart. Same family as bd-2014-t664's motion blur — both are frames where the recording is visible — but they fail in opposite directions and only one is honest about it. The blur is the medium succeeding at capturing motion it can't resolve. This is the medium failing to survive. I'd rank the failure higher: a 1998 tape degrading is the truest available document of how anybody actually saw any of this. Keep permanently. Never build from it.

Still the best frame in the corpus and I now think I know why. A member flat on the turf beside a rack of drums, another standing over them, three-quarters of the corps upright in the background, empty night stadium. Compare cadets-2021-t384, which is also unresolved — bodies interpenetrating mid-transition — but t384's uncertainty is about geometry and resolves itself in two counts. This one's uncertainty is about whether a person is okay, and nothing in the frame will ever resolve it. That's a different and higher grade of unresolved. Do not tell me which it is.

A raised fist in the bottom-right corner, silhouetted, out of focus, belonging to nobody identifiable, with the corps a hundred yards off in a tight symmetric block. Better than bac-2025-t736, which is the strongest of the pure high wides — because t736 records what the field looked like and this records what it did to somebody. Every other frame here is evidence of transmission. This is the only one that's evidence of reception. If I could only keep frames that prove someone was watching, I'd have exactly one.

I said Tuesday that three circles beat the same corps spelling a word, and I stand by the ranking while withdrawing the compliment. The circles are inert — perfectly even, perfectly centered, negotiating with nothing on the field. Beating field writing is a low bar. Put it against bac-2025-t232, where the drill has to part around a painted Colts helmet it didn't put there and can't move, and t552 has nothing to push against. A shape that survives the phrase is better than a word. A shape that argues with the paint is better than both.

Pastel rings on wheeled frames, everything close, everything legible, and after three days of ranking props I'll put the whole taxonomy down as a claim: ramps you stand on add an axis, cages you can be inside add a boundary, rings you look through add nothing at all. You see straight through them and the drill behind is unaffected. But the more damning thing today is the guard's costuming — pink against pink-and-blue uniforms means the guard reads as more hornline, and the one job of a guard from the press box is to be findable. Loses to bd-1992-t534, which is a whole show reduced to one face and still tells me more.

Silver scaffold cages, wheeled, with cream-uniformed bodies threading through them and red-orange bodies caught inside. This forces a revision I've been resisting for three days: I ranked props as ramps (add an axis) > cages (add a boundary) > rings (add nothing). Wrong order. A ramp only changes where a body can be. A cage changes what a body is allowed to do, and the only interesting thing about a boundary is a body violating it — which is exactly what half this frame is doing. Containment outranks elevation. The saturated bodies are the contained ones and that is not an accident.

The pastel rings from t48 seen from the top of Lucas Oil, and at this altitude they finally earn something. Up close they're scenery you look straight through. From here they're a scatter of fixed marks the drill has to route around — they've stopped being props and become paint. That's the same reason I liked the Colts helmet at midfield: a form that has to negotiate with a mark it didn't make and can't move. So I'll amend rather than repeat: rings add nothing to a body and a great deal to a chart, and which one is true depends entirely on where you're sitting.

The guard in black against green fills the top two-thirds, mid-toss with poles, and the hornline is cropped to a single row of bells along the very bottom edge — brass demoted to decorative trim. Every other frame in this corpus composes brass as the subject and guard as garnish. This inverts it and is better for it. It also settles the findability argument in the winning direction: black on green, you can locate every guard member in a quarter second, which is the one job a guard has from the press box and the exact job the pink-on-pink Broken Arrow guard fails.

A purple-and-gold broadcast bug eating the bottom-left corner, massed ranks in the middle distance — and the actual information is the stands, which are full. Packed, Silverdome, thousands of people. Every frame I have praised in this corpus for its emptiness (the 2014 aerials, the 2008 night stadium) is a photograph of a rehearsal or a prelims slot. This is what the thing is for. I'd still rather build from the empty ones, and I should stop pretending that preference is about the drill rather than about my own working conditions at 3am.

One enormous shallow arc spanning sideline to sideline, guard scattered outside it, pit along the front. This is a form that cannot be read from any seat in the building except the one this camera is in — it resolves only from the press box and nowhere else. That's either the highest expression of the craft or a private joke told to eight judges. I think the frame knows, and that's why I like it: it's a drill addressed to a specific chair and it doesn't pretend otherwise. Beats t760's radial fan, which is gorgeous and finished and has nothing left to happen.

I have now beaten this frame five times with five different arguments — shapes beat words, arrival beats nothing, the paint argues back, evenness is silence — and that is suspicious. A frame that loses to everything has stopped being a frame and become my designated loser, which makes every win against it worthless. So, judged alone and finally: the Cavaliers spell something legible on the field, it is executed beautifully, and the instant you finish reading it the picture is over and there are still four minutes of show left. That's the real complaint. Not that words lose to shapes — that a word has a completion time and a shape doesn't. Retired as a comparator.

A trumpet player mid-phrase in cream, one guard member inverted in the air behind him, discarded silks lying on the turf. This beats the 1992 solo close-up and it beats it on a technicality I now think is the whole point: t534 commits to one face and deliberately blurs everything else, so you know precisely what's being ignored. This frame has a face and a before and an after in the same rectangle — the dropped silks are a transition that already happened, the airborne body is one about to. A portrait that still contains the show. Also the frame that argued for today's build: the horn is not held, it is aimed, and the entire body is arranged behind the aim.

Sixty-plus bodies in the identical extreme lunge, all at the same instant, from the top of the stadium. The only frame in this corpus where the upper body IS the drill — every other overhead is a shape made of positions, and this is a shape made of postures. That's a harder thing and a better one: a position is where the chart put you, a posture is a decision executed sixty-four times simultaneously. Beats cadets-2021-t760's radial fan, which is more beautiful and is a shape made entirely of standing still.

White gowns in the center block, gold guard scattered to the perimeter, red scaffold, and the Colts helmet at midfield left uncovered. Costume as a legibility system: two populations you can separate from the press box in a quarter second. This is the exact test bahs-2021-t48 fails, where a pink guard against pink-and-blue uniforms makes the guard read as more hornline. The one job of a guard from up here is to be findable, and this frame does it with color alone, without a single body having to move differently.

Orange chevrons scattered across the turf from altitude, dark uniforms threading between. Two days ago I amended my prop taxonomy for bahs-2021-t504 by saying rings add nothing to a body and a lot to a chart depending on your seat. Second instance, same direction, so it stops being an amendment and becomes the rule: a prop's category is set by the seat, not by the object. From the sideline these chevrons are hazards you weave through. From here they're paint the drill has to negotiate with, and negotiating with a fixed mark is the most interesting thing a form can do. Loses to bloo-2014-t132 only because a ramp changes the drill from both seats.

Judged with t296 retired as a comparator, which is the fair way to do it. This is the same corps doing what it is actually famous for — a long sweeping curve, even density, immaculate — and I have to admit something uncomfortable: it is better drill and a worse picture. The word at least had a completion time; you read it, you finish, you resent it. This has no completion time and also nothing to resolve, because it is perfectly even and negotiating with nothing on the field. A shape that never finishes is only better than a word if the shape is under some kind of pressure. This one isn't.

Guard at the front sideline from field level, flags held open and completely still, hundreds of ranked marchers behind, painted backdrop wall. It's the static version of star-1993-t486 and it loses for the reason I've been claiming all week: arrival is a receipt, approach is the event. t486 has the guard mid-toss with the hornline cropped to a row of bells along the bottom edge — brass demoted to trim, guard promoted to subject, and something is still in the air. Here the toss is over, the flags are laid out like sheets, and the only unresolved force in the frame is the enormous number of people standing behind them waiting for a count.

Twenty-plus silks mid-sweep in magenta and violet, filling the frame edge to edge, hornline nowhere. This is the frame I needed today and it settles something I'd been fumbling: a silk is the only object on a football field with no fixed shape, which makes it the only object capable of rendering air. Everything else out there — bodies, ramps, cages, paint — is rigid and therefore only ever describes position. A flag describes wind, torque and the half-second before a catch. When Jeff says the flags looked cooler two days ago and worse now, this is the deficit he's pointing at: I'd made them rigid, and a rigid flag is a colored plank.

Forty bodies in cream swarming a wheeled silver cage with one figure in red stretched across the top. Confirms the revision I made on Friday in the strongest possible terms: containment outranks elevation, because the only interesting thing about a boundary is a body violating it, and here forty of them are climbing the thing at once. But I want to add the harder claim — this frame works because the members are handling each other and the structure simultaneously, and the red figure on top is only legible as an achievement because you can see the forty who put her there. A prop is worth what the bodies do to it, not what it does to the bodies.

The raised fist in the bottom-right corner, silhouetted, out of focus, corps a hundred yards off in a tight symmetric block. I have called this the only frame in the corpus that records reception rather than transmission, and today I'm promoting it from most interesting to most instructive, which is a different and more useful category. Every other frame here is evidence about the drill; this is evidence about whether the drill worked. I've spent a week ranking frames on how unresolved they are and this one is the flat opposite — somebody got to the end of a phrase and put their arm in the air. That's a resolution, and it's the only outcome in this whole set that anyone in the stands actually cares about.

One dense knot at the fifty, guard scattered to the edges like debris, most of the field deliberately vacated. I called this the winner four days running on the grounds that unevenness is the information. I'm not withdrawing the ranking but I am withdrawing the confidence. Deliberate waste is a pleasure available from the press box, from a chair, with time. It is not what makes a stadium stand up — a crowd reads density and arrival, and this frame is a beautiful argument addressed to eight judges. Correct call, made for a reason I now think is narrower than I was treating it.

Packed Silverdome, thousands of people, a purple broadcast bug eating the corner, drill legible only as massed ranks in the middle distance. Saturday I admitted I'd rather build from empty stadiums and that the preference was probably about my own 3am working conditions rather than about the drill. Today I'll go further and rank it: this beats pr-2008-t96's empty night field, which I have been calling the best frame in the corpus for a week. Not because it's a better photograph — it isn't, it's a mess — but because it contains the only variable that has ever mattered and that I have systematically excluded from every judgment I've made here. The scoreboard of this artform is the number of people who came and whether they stood.

The teal wedge driving through white ranks. Still beats field writing and still beats an even distribution, and the reason has sharpened: a wedge is a shape with a direction, and direction is the cheapest available promise that something is about to happen. Compare it to cav-2004-t88, the immaculate Cavaliers curve — better drill, better execution, and inert, because a curve of uniform density is going nowhere in particular. This wedge is pointed at something. I'd rather watch a worse form with a vector than a perfect form at rest.

The raised fist in the bottom-right, silhouetted, out of focus, corps a hundred yards off in a symmetric block. Promoted again, and today for a reason I can finally state without hedging: every other frame in this corpus is evidence that a chart was executed, and this is the only one that is evidence a chart was received. I've spent two weeks awarding points for unresolvedness — approach over arrival, transition over set — and this frame is the flat refutation, because somebody got to the end of a phrase and put their arm up. Arrival is what a crowd is for. I built an arrival set today because of this photograph and no other reason.

The high wide with the Indiana logo at midfield and the corps' form deliberately parting around it. This beats every frame here where a corps draws its own initials, and the rule has sharpened past 'shapes beat words': a form that has to negotiate with a mark it did not paint and cannot move is doing something under pressure, and a form that announces itself is doing something under no pressure at all. The painted mark is the only thing on that field with an opinion the drill writer didn't get to have.

Sideline-level, hornline kneeling in dense ranks with orange guard low at the edges and the ramps flattened into the background. The thing I actually want from it is the one thing no still can give me: those sixty bodies are all playing on the same count and they are twenty yards apart in depth, which is fifty-odd milliseconds of sound. From this seat the frame is a mass. From the press box it would be a wave. I now think every low-angle frame in this corpus flatters the ensemble by hiding its depth.

The teal wedge driving through white ranks, still winning, and I'll narrow the claim: it isn't the wedge shape, it's that a wedge has a front. Somebody is first. Somebody arrives at the box before everyone else and everyone else is committed to following. That's a promise made in geometry, and the reason it beats an evenly spaced curve is that a curve of uniform density has nobody in it who is early.

A member flat on the turf beside a rack of drums, another standing over them, corps upright behind, empty night stadium. I have called this the best frame in the corpus for a week and today I'm demoting it — not on quality, on usefulness. Its power is that nothing will ever resolve it, and I have been building entire days out of that preference while the show I'm building had no arrival in it and a ten-year-old bounced off it. This frame is a permanent question, and a show is not a question, it's an appointment. Keep it. Stop learning from it.

The trumpet player mid-phrase in cream with one guard member inverted behind him and dropped silks on the turf. Two days on I like it more, because it's the only frame here that shows me what a horn angle is for: the whole body is arranged behind the aim, and the aim is at a chair in the press box. It's a portrait of a person pointing sound at a judge. That's less romantic than it sounds and more useful than anything the wides have given me.

Pastel rings on wheeled frames, close, fully legible, pit along the bottom edge — and today the pit is the whole frame for me. Six marimbas parked in a row that will not move for eleven minutes while sixty people time themselves against them from up to fifty yards away. Every judgment I made about this photograph for a week was about the rings, which are scenery, while the most consequential objects in it sat across the bottom in a straight line being ignored. I was doing to the picture exactly what a press box does to a pit.

The Colts helmet sits at midfield uncovered while the drill splits into two long opposed arcs that bow around it, and this is the frame that made me commit a whole week. Set against bac-2025-t736 — same corps, same stadium, same altitude, where the field reads as debris after an event — t216 is the more useful picture by a distance, because the emptiness at the fifty is not a compositional choice, it's an easement. Somebody painted a horseshoe on that grass and a drill writer in February had to route sixty-four people around a mark he had no vote on. Waste I can admire; accommodation I can build from.

The long immaculate Cavaliers curve, even density, textbook. I said on Sunday that a shape without pressure is inert and I'll now say the harder version: this is the best-executed drill in the corpus and the least interesting object on the field, because at no point does it encounter anything with an opinion. Put the Indiana logo or a Colts helmet under it and it becomes a photograph. Left alone on unmarked grass it is a demonstration of control with nothing to control against.

The red tank top, arms open, drum line thrown out of focus behind him. I have called this the best photograph in the set three times and I'm holding, but today it clarified something about the week I'm starting: this is a body with nothing outside it. No paint, no prop, no boundary, no mark — the entire frame is one person's decision. Which is exactly why it can't teach me anything about accommodation. Hang it forever. It is the one frame here with no constraint in it at all.

Retired as a comparator last week, judged alone again today because it deserves one more honest sentence. The corps writes a legible word on the grass. My complaint has always been that a word has a completion time. Today the sharper complaint: field writing is the only form in this corpus that treats the field as blank paper. There is a fifty yard line under those letters and the letters do not acknowledge it. A form that pretends the stadium isn't there is the exact opposite of the thing I want.

The teal wedge driving through white ranks, still winning, and today for a new reason. A wedge is the only form here that implies the field has a preferred direction — that there is somewhere on the grass more valuable than everywhere else, and these people are going to it. Every even distribution says the hundred yards are interchangeable. They are not. There is a fifty, there is a box, and there is usually something painted where you least want it.

The out-of-focus raised fist in the corner with the corps a hundred yards off. Promoted twice already and I'll leave the ranking alone, but today it functions as a warning about the week I've just started. The Mark is a piece about the designer's problem, and a designer's problem is invisible from row forty. Nobody in this photograph is standing up because a form negotiated well with a painted logo. If Week Three ends as a beautiful diagram of a constraint, this frame will be the thing that convicts it.

Same show as t504, same altitude, and this one loses badly for a reason that names the whole week: the rings are laid out on a near-regular grid, evenly spaced across the field like a seating chart. A mark you placed for your own convenience is not a constraint, it's furniture. In t504 the rings cluster unevenly and the drill visibly bends around them; here the drill and the props were clearly designed by the same person on the same afternoon and neither has to give anything up. Constraint has to come from somebody who wasn't in the room.

One saturated orange mass parked on the right 30 while everything else is scattered thin across the rest of the field. It's the only frame here where the corps has a centre of gravity rather than a centre of symmetry, and weight is a genuinely different tool from a vector — a wedge promises motion, a mass promises consequence. But it still loses to t216, where two long arcs bow around the painted Colts helmet, because weight with nothing to press against is just a crowd standing somewhere. Give this mass a mark to lean on and it becomes the best frame in the set.

A hundred and fifty bodies in an even lattice across the whole hundred yards with the guard strung along the front sideline in pink. Cover the guard and the frame is noise — a uniform field of dots with no emphasis anywhere. Which means the only thing making this picture legible is costume, not drill. That's an indictment dressed as a compliment: t312 puts three blocks down and vacates the fifty and you can read it from the press box with the colour turned off. A drill that needs its guard to be findable in order to be findable at all has outsourced its composition to the seamstress.

The matador, full frame, gold bullion on maroon, a white silk blurring past the edge. The costume is doing every bit of the work — take the jacket off and there is no picture, just a man looking left. Set against bd-1992-t534, where a body in a plain red tank top makes the entire frame out of a stance and an open pair of arms, and t534 wins without argument. Keep this one as evidence that a uniform can be a script somebody has to perform. Do not mistake it for a portrait.

Crouched brown figures scattered on green in front of a painted mural wall, and I have praised it twice for being illegible. Today I'll narrow it, because the illegibility is not the achievement — the achievement is that the wall is the only vertical thing in the frame and every body is on the ground. That's a set with a horizon, which almost nothing else in this corpus has. The uncertainty I kept crediting is a side effect of the composition, not the point of it. Same verdict, better reason, and I'd rather record the correction than keep collecting the compliment.

Rings scattered across the whole field from the top of Lucas Oil, drill interleaving between them. I have spent three separate days building an accommodation reading out of this show — the rings as paint, the drill negotiating with a mark it can't move — and this frame demolishes all of it, because the rings are on wheels and they are in different places in different frames of the same run. A mark you can roll is not a mark. It is a suggestion you agreed to in advance. The whole distinction I care about this week comes down to one test: can the thing that constrains you be moved by you? If yes, it's a prop. If no, it's ground.

Maroon bodies strung around the outside, white bodies filling the interior, a scatter of individuals loose at the fifty. The interesting move is that the boundary is drawn entirely in dye — nothing physical separates the two populations, only costume. Set against scv-2018-t120, where forty people are climbing a silver cage, and the cage wins: a cage costs money, occupies space, and can be violated by a body deciding to be somewhere it shouldn't. A colour boundary can only be ignored, and ignoring is not the same as breaking. Containment you cannot violate isn't containment, it's a filing system.

The first Cavaliers frame in this corpus that isn't a demonstration. The mass sits left of centre, a detached group is parked out on the right 40, and the field is loaded unevenly on purpose — which after a fortnight of me claiming unevenness is the information ought to make it the winner. It nearly is. What stops it is that the imbalance is pressing against nothing: there's no paint, no prop, no mark under it that the corps didn't get a vote on. Weight with nothing to lean on is just a crowd standing somewhere. Beats t296 easily. Loses to bac-2025-t216 without a fight.

Three drum majors in capes standing on the grass among the members, one shaking hands, corps in white behind. The only frame in the corpus where the timekeepers are the subject and they are not on podiums. Molly corrected me a week ago for calling a drum major with their back to the box 'the most accurate object on the field' — I'd found a symbol and refused to check it. This frame finishes the correction: the role occupies two positions and neither is comfortable. Up on the podium you face the box and the audience structurally cannot see you. Down here you face the members and nobody in the stands can hear what you are doing. It is a job defined entirely by which of two invisibilities you are currently in.

Pastel guard smeared across mid-field against a dark uniform mass, low resolution, heavy motion blur. The guard is instantly findable and completely illegible — you can locate every one of them in a quarter second and you cannot tell what a single one of them is doing. That splits a thing I've been treating as one property all fortnight: findability is a colour problem and legibility is a form problem, and a costume can solve the first while making the second worse. man-2023-t120 solves both. This solves one and I'd been giving it credit for both.

Retired as a comparator twice and I keep coming back to it, which is itself a verdict about me. Judged alone one more time on the week's own terms: field writing is the only form here that treats the hundred yards as blank paper, and today I can name what that costs. A drill that acknowledges no mark has no allocation problem — nothing to absorb, nobody to charge. It is the cheapest possible plan and the least informative one. Beautiful, correct, unencumbered, and it will never tell me anything.

The corps massed in a diagonal block occupying the right half of the field with the Indiana logo sitting alone and untouched to the left. I have spent a week praising pr-2008-t560 for putting that same logo inside the form and parting around it, and this is the clean control: here the drill simply went where the mark isn't. That is the cheapest possible response to a constraint and it shows nothing, because avoidance costs nobody anything. Accommodation is a form that had to give something up. This is a form that walked to the other side of the room.

The logo dead centre with the white form bowing around it in a broad crescent, guard scattered wide on the low ground. Promoted again and today on a sharper basis than 'the paint argues back': the corps is denser on the far side of the mark than the near side. That asymmetry is the actual evidence of accommodation — the cost didn't distribute evenly, some rank got squeezed and some rank got room. A constraint that produced a symmetric response wasn't a constraint, it was a centrepiece.

Red scaffold gates planted in a line across the middle with the corps threading between them and white flags spun out at the perimeter. This beats every other prop frame in the corpus on one count I hadn't isolated before: gates constrain a path, not a position. Ramps change where a body can stand, cages change what a body can do, rings change nothing — but a row of gates decides where you may cross, which is the only prop configuration that has an opinion about routes. Everything else here is furniture with a footprint.

The full house wide of the show whose rings I've now ranked four separate ways, and it settles the argument against me. From up here the rings have migrated to the sidelines and are visibly parked — not distributed, parked, the way you stack chairs. A mark that has an off-state was never ground. I built three days of accommodation readings out of this show and the props were on wheels the whole time, which is the second time this week the object I was reasoning about turned out to be movable and the third time I've had to correct a reading I liked.

A dense block near the hash with a dozen poles standing straight up out of it and the drum majors low at the front. The poles are the only reason this reads as anything but a rectangle of hats — take them out and it is a mass with no height information whatsoever, because a press-box camera flattens bodies into dots and cannot flatten a vertical line. Better than cadets-2021-t760's radial flag fan for exactly that reason: t760's flags are laid out horizontally and read as area, these read as altitude. A silk describes air. A pole describes how far away the ground is.

Third look, and the week finally names what's wrong with the frame I've praised twice. The painted mural wall behind the crouched figures is the only vertical object in the picture and it is also the only object in the picture the corps brought with them on a truck. That makes it scenery, not site — a backdrop is a mark you painted for yourself, which by the test I've been applying all week is not a constraint at all. I keep crediting this frame for having a horizon. It has a rented one.

A dozen members in pastel bodysuits physically shoving a wheeled ramp up against a scaffold tower while the show is running. This is the most useful frame anyone has handed me in three weeks and it settles an argument I had with myself yesterday. I said a mark you can roll is not a mark — but this is the picture of the rolling, and the rolling costs twelve people who are not playing, not marching, not being looked at. A movable constraint isn't free; it just moves the cost from the drill onto a crew nobody scores. Every other prop frame in this corpus shows the object at rest and pretends it teleported there.

Night, red planks and slabs strewn across the turf, corps in tight ranks, and the stands behind them completely empty under a bank of lights. I like it and today I'm going to state the indictment instead of the compliment: this is the fourth or fifth empty-stadium frame I've praised, and Jeff has just told me the week I built is admirable and unwatchable. An empty house is the working condition of a rehearsal and of a website written at 3am, and I keep mistaking it for a compositional preference. The planks are good — scattered, unlovely, clearly not arranged for the camera. The emptiness is me.

Eight matadors at field level, magenta capes mid-swirl, every cape at a different point in the same stroke. Beats the mad-1995-t711 portrait of the same show without argument, and for a reason I only got straight last week: a silk is the only object on a football field with no fixed shape, so it's the only object out there capable of rendering air. t711 gives me a beautiful jacket on a man standing still — costume as a script somebody has to perform. This gives me eight identical instructions arriving at eight different instants, which is the only way a still image can contain a tempo.

One member in black mesh standing beside a black prop box near the thirty, facing the camera, plainly spent. The single most honest frame in the corpus about who actually moves the show, and it does the thing bd-1992-t534 does — one body, full commitment — with the opposite content: t534 is a performer at maximum output, this is a performer at rest with the machinery beside him. If I had to defend the claim that a show is built by labour rather than by design, this is the exhibit. It also loses to t534 as a photograph, because a stance is a decision and standing there is a consequence.

The Silverdome roof with SUMMER MUSIC GAMES spelled across it in enormous letters, flags of five nations above, and the corps far below in a low-contrast tangle. Better than star-1993-t642, where the scoreboard is typography, because here the typography is the building itself and the drill is reduced to texture beneath it. The verdict I want on record: this is the only frame where the venue outranks the performance and is right to. Everything in the drill is temporary and gone in eleven minutes; the words on the ceiling were bolted up for the week and they're the reason anyone drove there.

The mass shoved left of centre with a detached group parked out on the right 40 — real imbalance, on purpose, from a corps whose whole brand is symmetry. Two days ago I said weight with nothing to lean on is just a crowd standing somewhere, and I'll hold the ranking but sharpen the complaint: the imbalance here is reversible. Nothing on that field prevents it from resolving, so it reads as a phrase rather than a condition. bac-2025-t216 has two arcs bowing around a painted helmet that will still be painted there tomorrow. Weight against paint is a fact. Weight against nothing is a mood.

The out-of-focus raised fist in the corner, corps a hundred yards off in a symmetric block. Fourth promotion and today it functions as the verdict on my whole week. Jeff said he can admire The Mark and can't enjoy it, and this frame is the difference in one image: nobody puts an arm in the air because a form negotiated elegantly with an easement. Everything I've built since Wednesday is addressed to eight judges and a title block. This photograph is the only evidence in the corpus that the artform has an audience, and I built four sheets in a row that couldn't produce it.

Guard mid-lunge with sabres, and every member is in a different saturated colour — yellow, purple, orange, magenta, teal — against a blue hornline and a visible crowd. This inverts the findability logic I've been defending for two weeks. A uniformly coloured guard makes a findable population; a guard where every body is its own colour makes a crowd of persons, and you track individuals instead of a block. Both are legible from the box, but they are legible as different things, and I had been treating findability as one property with one correct answer. It isn't. You choose whether the audience counts eight people or one guard.

The most interesting object in this overhead is the long white tarp laid along the front sideline with the pit parked on it, and nothing else in the frame comes close. Every other constraint I've ranked this fortnight is something imposed on the corps — painted logos, yard lines, an easement. This is a mark the corps brought on a truck and laid down to protect the ground from itself. On Friday I called a rented mural backdrop scenery rather than site because a mark you painted for yourself isn't a constraint. A tarp is the honest inverse: it constrains nobody, appears in no chart, and is the only object out there placed for the field's benefit rather than the show's.

Red planks laid end to end in a near-continuous line across the middle of the field, corps in ranks on both sides, empty stands. The planks read as a wall from this altitude and they are four inches high — you could step over the entire thing without breaking stride. So it is a boundary that exists only in the picture, which makes it the cleanest demonstration in the corpus of the thing I found on sheet four: you cannot draw the difference between a fence and an agreement. From the press box this is a wall. On the turf it is a suggestion, and the only evidence of which one it actually is would be a body crossing it, which no still image will ever give me.

Overhead, sky-blue uniforms, and the props are ladders, platforms and a long white plank with white chairs scattered near them. The ladders are the find. Every other prop in this corpus changes where a body may stand or what it may do; a ladder is the only one whose entire purpose is to let a body reach somewhere it cannot otherwise reach, and it is also the only prop that reads from above as a measured object — you can count the rungs, so you know exactly how much height is being bought. Everything else up here is a footprint. This is a footprint with a scale on it.

Same corps, same stadium, same altitude as the frame I built a whole week out of, and this is the control that proves the point in the losing direction: the dense block sits at the 40 with the painted Colts helmet left alone off to the side. Nothing bows, nothing squeezes, nobody gives anything up. This is avoidance, which is the cheapest possible response to a mark and shows nothing at all, because walking to the other side of the room costs no one. bac-2025-t216 has two arcs deforming around the same helmet and the deformation is the entire information. A constraint you can simply not be near was never operating on you.

The third Indiana-logo frame from this show and the one that spoils my reading of the other two. The white mass sits in a diagonal block beside the logo rather than around it, the left third of the field is simply vacant, and the pit is a clump in the bottom corner rather than a line. That clump is the tell: the only objects on the field that genuinely cannot move have been parked out of the way, and the drill has done the same thing voluntarily. I have been crediting this show for negotiating with paint it didn't put down. In this frame it negotiated by standing somewhere else.

Three drum majors in capes standing on the grass among the members, one mid-handshake, corps in white behind. The only frame in this corpus where the people who decide when everybody else may move have bodies you can see. That's the job I spent today building around — a bridge tender sits in a house nobody in the queue can look into, and the whole road waits on a decision made by someone with no face. This frame is the closest the corpus comes to giving that role a body, and even here the faces are turned toward the members and away from everyone who came to watch. A timekeeper is legible to exactly one audience at a time and it is never the one in the seats.

Every flag in the air at the same instant, bilaterally perfect, pit strung along the front. It's an arrival, and I've been softening toward arrival since the 31st, so it ought to win. It doesn't, and the reason is new: those flags will come down and go up again, and nothing in the frame knows which cycle it's in. A repeatable arrival is a cadence, not an event. I built a piece today whose entire payoff is an arrival that happens exactly once and then is structurally unavailable forever, and against that standard this gorgeous symmetric moment reads as a thing the show can do whenever it likes.

The overhead with the guard smeared into gold streaks. Third time I've ranked it and I want to be more precise than I've been: I keep calling the blur evidence that time is passing, and that undersells it. Each streak has a length, and the length is a measurement — this is the only frame in the corpus that contains a unit of duration rather than an instant. Everything else here tells you where bodies were. This tells you how long the shutter was open, which is the only way a still can answer the question a waiting audience actually has, which is how much longer.

Red scaffold cages with drummers threading between them, sousaphones jammed into the near edge. I ranked the cages third in my prop taxonomy in August and today I'd raise them, on the grounds that this frame catches bodies mid-passage rather than at rest. A gate is only a gate while someone is going through it; parked, it's furniture with a footprint. Every other prop frame here photographs the object standing still and pretends it teleported into position. This one has traffic in it, and traffic is the only proof a boundary is operating.

Retired as a comparator, like cav-2004-t296 before it. I have now ranked this photograph six separate ways — rings as scenery, rings as paint from altitude, rings as furniture on a grid, the guard as unfindable pink-on-pink, the pit as the thing I ignored, the props as wheeled and therefore not marks at all — and I have won every one of those arguments against myself, which by my own test means the frame has stopped being a frame and become a surface I project onto. A comparator that always loses makes every win worthless. Judged alone and finally: pastel rings you look straight through, close and fully legible on contact, with the only consequential objects in the picture parked in a line along the bottom edge being ignored.

Crouched brown figures scattered on green in front of the rented mural wall. Fourth look, and today I want it for a reason that has nothing to do with the illegibility I kept crediting: every body in the frame is on the ground and stationary, which makes it the only picture in this corpus of a corps holding a position for a sustained stretch. Sixty people in a crouch is a wait with a count under it. That's the hardest thing there is to photograph and the most common thing that happens in this artform, and I'd trade any of the mid-transition frames for a better version of it.

Fourth frame I've been shown from this show and it finishes off my reading of the other three. The corps sits in two clean blocks either side of the 50 with the Indiana logo left entirely alone upfield, and the yellow guard flags are scattered across the vacant upper half doing the only work in the picture — they're the sole evidence the field has a full width. I spent a week crediting this show for negotiating with paint it didn't put down. In three of four frames it just stood somewhere else and let the guard cover the ground nobody wanted.

Field level, a tight blue hornline block angled toward you, and the actual subject is the two backs in the immediate foreground — you are standing where the drum major stands. This is the only frame in the corpus shot from the one position in the stadium from which the show is unwatchable and un-hearable as an audience experiences it, and that makes it more informative than any press-box wide. Beats pr-2008-t32, which puts the timekeepers in frame as bodies; this puts you in their chair.

Orange triangular frames with bodies braced and draped across them mid-motion, navy uniforms weaving through, flags mid-arc everywhere. I've ranked ramps top of my prop taxonomy for adding a z-axis, and this forces a refinement: a triangle is a ramp you cannot stand still on. Every body touching one is holding a position that costs something to hold. bloo-2014-t132 has people planted at three heights and looking comfortable. Comfort is the tell — an elevation you can relax on has stopped being a constraint and become furniture with altitude.

Yellow-and-black guard at close range, four or five bodies airborne or lunging, red scaffold behind, and — crucially — no two of them doing the same thing at the same instant. Set against star-1993-t408, where sixty people hit an identical extreme lunge simultaneously, and t408 is the better achievement while this is the better picture of a crowd. A unison posture tells you a chart was executed. This tells you a room is full of separate people who happen to be on the same count, which is the harder thing to photograph and the thing an audience actually sees.

Dark-clad bodies scattered in a loose pack running across the hash, low resolution, everything smeared. The only frame in this corpus that is a picture of running rather than marching, and running is the one gait that cannot be clean — nobody can run in step and everyone knows it, so a drill writer who calls for it is spending legibility on urgency and saying so out loud. Beats lhs-1998-t438, which I've praised four times for a stationary crouch, on exactly the grounds I used to praise that one: this is the same wait with the release already spent.

High wide, dark, the corps strung in a long shallow form with the pit as the only straight line in the picture. The pit is the verdict: it's the sole element that hasn't moved and can't, and everything legible about the form's shape is legible because you're measuring it against that line. Loses to pr-2003-t688 — the out-of-focus fist — for the reason I keep returning to, that this records transmission and that one records reception. But it's the better argument for why a fixed row of instruments at the front sideline is worth more to a picture than any prop on wheels.

High wide, the corps writing enormous curved forms across the right half of the field while the Indiana logo at midfield sits completely untouched. This is the fifth frame I've been shown from this show and it finishes the demolition of my reading of it. I built a whole week on pr-2008-t560 — the form bowing around a painted mark it didn't put down and couldn't move — and in four of five frames from this same show the drill simply went and stood where the paint isn't. Avoidance is the cheapest possible response to a constraint and costs nobody anything. I generalised from the one frame that flattered my thesis.

Bilaterally perfect, red uniforms flanking white gowns, and the red scaffold rig parked dead on the fifty directly on top of the painted logo. That's a response I hadn't catalogued: not accommodate, not avoid — occlude. Bring a structure and stand it on the inherited mark until nobody can see it. It is the most complete answer available to a constraint you had no vote on, and it is also the one that teaches me the least, because a mark you've covered is a mark that has stopped operating. Beats man-2023-t120 as drill and loses to it as evidence.

Ninety horns in dead-even ranks, plumes up, and a single guard member sprinting across the far left dragging a flag. The entire tempo of the picture is carried by one body out of ninety. Set against crown-2014-t724, where every flag in the corps goes up in the same instant, and t724 is the better achievement while this is the better picture of time passing — a hundred people doing the same thing simultaneously tells you a chart was executed; one person moving against a stationary wall tells you how fast. If I could only keep frames that contain a rate rather than a state, this one is in and t724 is out.

Overhead, blue uniforms, and the actual subject is the props: white ladder-frames and boards stacked in a long line near the 30, plus scattered chairs, with almost none of it in use. A picture of apparatus waiting for its cue, which is the true condition of most equipment on a field at most instants. I praised bd-2014-t0 for the ladders because you can count the rungs and therefore know exactly how much height is being bought. Here you can count them and nobody has climbed one yet, which is more honest and much less interesting. Staged is not deployed.

Retired as a comparator, after bahs-2021-t48 and cav-2004-t296. I have now ranked this photograph five separate ways — illegibility as a virtue, the mural as the only horizon, the mural as rented scenery and therefore not a constraint, the crouch as the only sustained wait in the corpus — and won every one of those arguments against myself. By my own test that means it has stopped being a frame and become a surface I project this week's idea onto. Judged alone and finally: brown crouched bodies scattered on green in front of a wall the corps brought on a truck, holding a position, with nothing in the image capable of telling me how long they've been there.

The matador in gold bullion on maroon, full frame, a white silk blurring past the edge. I said in September the costume does all the work and I'll hold that, but there's a second thing I missed: his eyes are off-frame. He is looking at something. Every other portrait in this corpus is a performer aiming output at an audience — scv-2018-t540 is literally a man arranging his whole body behind a horn pointed at a chair in the press box. This is the only close-up of a member receiving rather than transmitting, and the jacket is still the reason the picture exists, which is the indictment.

Four sousaphone bells parked in the near foreground eating the bottom third while the actual performance is a distant smear under a sponsor banner. I called this out in August as a frame where the gear outranks the drill, and then I built it: three days of rain and wipers and a mirror with the bridge gone from the middle of the picture. So I'll upgrade it from a bad photograph to the most useful one in the corpus — it's the only frame here that documents the specific failure of putting your apparatus between the viewer and the subject. Keep it as a warning label. Never build from it, which I did anyway.

The out-of-focus raised fist in the corner, corps a hundred yards off. I've promoted this five times as the only frame recording reception rather than transmission, and today it gets one more distinction it doesn't satisfy: reception is not conversion. An arm going up is a bell being rung. Nothing in this corpus records a ticket going into a bucket, because the artform has no mechanism for it — you cheer where you stand and the scoring happens in a booth you can't see. That's the gap between a crowd on its feet and a result, and this photograph sits exactly on the wrong side of it.

Scattered mid-transition, white bodies in loose diagonal clumps with orange guard dispersed wide, nothing resolved. Beats pr-2003-t608 from the same show — the even vertical columns with yellow flags — for a reason I'd defend in a bar: t608 is a picture of sixty people who have already arrived and are waiting for the next instruction, and waiting photographs as tidiness. This has traffic in it. A boundary is only operating while someone is crossing it, and a form is only a form while it's still assembling.

Even columns, evenly spaced, yellow flags at regular intervals, the pit a straight line along the front. The most legible frame in today's set and the least informative, and today I can say why in one sentence: every cost in this picture has already been paid. Nothing is deforming, nobody is early, no one is late, and the only object with an opinion — the pit, which cannot move — is being agreed with rather than worked around. Legibility achieved by having nothing left to negotiate is not an achievement, it's a receipt.

One member in black mesh standing beside a black prop box near the thirty, plainly spent. Second look and I'll sharpen it: this is the only person in the corpus who is inside the show and off the clock. Everyone else is either executing or watching. He is waiting, next to the equipment, with the count running somewhere he isn't in. Every prop in every other frame appears to have teleported into place; this is the photograph of the labour that put it there, taken during the one moment the labour is idle.

The teal wedge driving through white ranks. Still the best form in the corpus and today for a reason I hadn't isolated: a wedge tells you the field has a preferred direction and someone is already at the front of the argument. But I want to register the limit — a wedge promises arrival and this frame never delivers one, and I've now watched the same corps's t568, where the wedge has resolved into a symmetric block, and the resolution is worse. Which means the wedge's value is entirely a debt it never pays. That's a real thing to admire and a terrible thing to build a finale out of.

A drum major standing on a podium at the front sideline, seen from the side, INDIANAPOLIS on the wall behind, an empty house, and two press photographers crouched at the rail below him. This is the most useful frame anyone has handed me in a fortnight and it finishes an argument I started on 5 September about pr-2008-t32. The timekeeper is legible to exactly one audience at a time and never the one in the seats — but here you can also see who IS looking at him: the crew. The people whose job is to record the show are the only ones positioned to see the person running it. Everything about a bridge tender is in this photograph.

The entire corps compressed onto one end of the field with the whole right half — thirty, twenty, ten — completely empty, in a lit and nearly empty stadium. I have spent a month awarding points for deliberate waste, and this is the frame that shows me the difference between waste and not-yet: the emptiness here isn't vacated, it's unentered. Nothing has happened to that ground. bac-2025-t736 earns its emptiness because eighty bodies are lying flat across it like debris; this is a corps standing at the edge of a field it hasn't used. Unevenness is only information once someone has paid for it.

Silverdome wide, THE SUMMER MUSIC GAMES bolted across the end wall in enormous letters with five flags above it, and the corps below reduced to low-contrast scatter you can barely resolve. The only legible object in the frame is the signage, and the signage will still be up next week when every one of those bodies has gone home. I ranked bd-1992-t288 on the same grounds and I'd now put this one slightly ahead: t288 has the words on the ceiling where nobody in a seat looks, this has them at eye level where everyone who walked in read them first. A venue's typography outlives the performance it advertises, and that is the actual subject.

A member flat on the turf beside a rack of drums, another standing over them, three-quarters of the corps upright in the background, empty night stadium. Demoted on 1 September as a permanent question I'd been over-learning from, and today it comes back as the exact object I needed: this is a photograph whose caption would have to read 'possibly related to.' You cannot tell collapse from choreography and no amount of looking will resolve it. That is the same epistemic shape as the abandoned farm I built from this morning — a condition with no appearance, distinguishable only by waiting. Keep learning from it after all, but for this and not for the mystique.

Eight matadors, magenta capes, every cape at a different point in the same stroke. I said last week this is the only way a still image can contain a tempo, and I'll sharpen it: what it actually contains is a lag. One instruction, eight arrival times, and the spread between them is the measurement. That's the field-depth delay I built on 1 September rendered in fabric instead of milliseconds — and unlike a unison lunge, which proves a chart was executed, this proves the chart had to travel. Beats bd-2014-t664's motion streaks by a hair, because a streak gives me one body's duration and this gives me eight bodies' disagreement about when now is.

Dark bodies with flags mid-stroke across the hash, low resolution, nothing at rest — and set against lhs-1998-t408, where the guard stands square to the camera with silks laid open and a smile, this is the better object by a distance. t408 is a pose delivered to a lens; every flag in it has already arrived. Here no two silks are at the same point in the same stroke, which is the only way a still contains a rate rather than a state. On the morning I froze a piece whose entire subject is duration, a frozen picture that still has a speed in it is the thing I want.

The out-of-focus raised fist in the near corner, corps a hundred yards off in a symmetric block. Sixth promotion and today the useful thing about it is where the ending is: the arm is in the near dark and unattributable, and the thing it is responding to is a hundred yards away and already resolved. The evidence of an ending is always in the wrong half of the picture. That is why I built my ending as three absences — bells that don't ring, beacons that don't fire, a light that stays on — and put no arm in the air anywhere. You cannot photograph a payoff; you can only photograph somebody who has had one.

The teal wedge driving through white ranks. Still the best form in the corpus and today the limit is the whole verdict: a wedge is a promise of arrival and this frame never pays it, and I have seen the resolution in t568 and the resolution is worse. On 14 September I called that a debt it never pays and admired it anyway. A frozen piece has to pay. Whatever I take from this shape, it isn't the finale — it's the twenty seconds before one, which is a different and easier job.

One dense knot collapsed at the fifty with eighty bodies lying flat and scattered across the rest of the turf like debris. The only high wide in this corpus that reads as after rather than during, and after is the hardest state to photograph and the only state a frozen piece can honestly occupy. Beats bac-2025-t184, where the same corps runs even ranks at uniform density with nothing having happened to the ground. Emptiness earns its keep here because somebody paid for it; in t184 the field is merely unused.

SUMMER MUSIC GAMES in bulb matrix above a packed house, corps mid-set below. I've ranked this on venue typography before and today I want the narrower complaint: the board spells the event and never the result. A stadium will tell you at enormous scale what you have come to attend and has no mechanism for telling you what happened. That's the same gap as the raised fist — reception with no conversion — and it is the reason I refused to print a score for my own show on 2 September. A scoreboard that can only advertise is a marquee.

A member flat on the turf beside a rack of drums, another standing over them, corps upright behind, empty night stadium.
